english: Qi never bribed Qin, yet in the end followed the five states into extinction. Why?
Because it allied with Qin and did not aid the five states.
Once the five states were lost, Qi too could not escape.
The lords of Yan and Zhao at first had far-reaching strategy, could hold their land, and in righteousness refused to bribe Qin.
Hence Yan, though a small state, fell last—the effect of its use of arms.
But when Dan resorted to the Jing Ke plot, calamity came swiftly.
Zhao had fought Qin five times, losing twice and winning thrice.
Afterwards Qin attacked Zhao twice more, and Li Mu twice repulsed it.
After Li Mu was put to death on a slander and Handan became a commandery, it was pitiable that Zhao's use of arms came to no good end.
Moreover, Yan and Zhao stood at the moment when Qin's extirpation of the other states was nearly complete—strategically isolated and weak, their fall in defeat was truly beyond remedy.

Had the three states each loved their land, had Qi not cleaved to Qin, the assassin not gone forth, the good general still stood—then victory or defeat, survival or ruin, matched against Qin, might well have proved otherwise.

Had the lands given to Qin been used to enfeoff the empire's strategists, and the heart that served Qin been turned to honour the empire's uncommon talents, with all strength turned westward, I fear the men of Qin could not have swallowed their meal.
With such an advantage, yet terrorised by Qin's accumulated might, they were pared daily, carved monthly, drifting toward ruin.
Those who rule states—let them never be terrorised by accumulated might!
The Six States and Qin were all feudal lords; their power weaker than Qin's, yet they still had the potential to defeat it without bribing.
If one rules the whole empire yet follows the old story of the Six States' ruin, that is to place oneself below the Six States.

Duke Xiao of Qin, holding the fastness of Xiao and Han and possessing the land of Yongzhou, with ruler and ministers firmly guarding and eyeing the Zhou court, cherished the ambition to sweep up the world, wrap up the whole realm, gather in the four seas, and swallow the eight wilds.

At that time Lord Shang aided him: within, he established laws and statutes, devoted to ploughing and weaving, and prepared implements of defence and war; without, he formed the Lianheng alliance and set the lords against one another.

After Duke Xiao died, Huiwen, Wu and Zhaoxiang inherited the old enterprise and followed the bequeathed strategies: south they seized Hanzhong, west they took Ba and Shu, east they cut away fertile lands, north they gathered in the crucial commanderies.
Not stinting precious vessels, treasures, and rich lands, they gathered the talents of the world, who bound themselves in the North-South alliance and became as one.

These four lords were all wise, intelligent, loyal and trustworthy, generous and loving, honouring the worthy and valuing men of worth; they formed the Vertical alliance and broke the Horizontal, mustering the multitudes of Han, Wei, Yan, Chu, Qi, Zhao, Song, Wei and Zhongshan.
With tenfold the land and hosts of a million, they knocked at the pass to attack Qin.
The men of Qin opened the pass to receive the enemy, yet the armies of the nine states hesitated and dared not advance.
Qin had spent not an arrow or a bolt, yet the lords of the world were already exhausted.
Qin had strength to spare to exploit their weaknesses, pursued the fleeing and routed, with a million corpses and blood enough to float shields.
Turning advantage to profit, it carved up the world and split the rivers and mountains.
Strong states begged submission; weak states entered Qin's court.
Passing to Xiaowen and Zhuangxiang, their reigns were brief, and the state knew no alarm.

Then came the First Emperor: kindling the fierce legacy of six generations, he cracked the long whip to drive the universe, swallowed the Two Zhous and destroyed the lords, mounted the supreme throne and ruled the Six Directions, clutched the rod of chastisement and flogged the world—his might shook the four seas.
South he seized the lands of the Baiyue, making them the commanderies of Guilin and Xiang;
the lords of the Baiyue bowed their heads, ropes about their necks, committing their lives to the petty officials.
Then he sent Meng Tian north to build the Great Wall and hold the frontier fence, pushing back the Xiongnu seven hundred li;
the Hu dared not come south to graze their horses, and warriors dared not bend the bow to avenge their wrongs.
He razed famous cities, slaughtered heroes;
collected the arms of the world, gathered them at Xianyang, melted blades and arrowheads, and cast them into twelve golden giants, thereby weakening the people of the world.
Then he made Mount Hua his wall and the Yellow River his moat, holding the city walls a hundred million feet high and looking down on the fathomless deep, deeming it secure.
